name: कर्मसंन्यासयोग
teaching: Asked to choose between renouncing action and performing it, Krishna refuses the choice: both lead to freedom, but acting without attachment is the more honest road. True renunciation is inner — the knower acts, yet holds 'I do nothing at all.' Equanimity, not abstention, is the mark of the free. The quarrel between renouncing and acting is dissolved from the inside: both paths meet in the one who works with offered hands and a lotus-leaf heart. Peace, the chapter insists, is found knowing the Friend of all beings.
questions: What have you given up outwardly while still gripping it inwardly?
Could you do today's most tedious task as if you were not its doer?
Where do you still divide the world into what elevates you and what is beneath you?

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
संन्यासं कर्मणां कृष्ण पुनर्योगं च शंससि ।
यच्छ्रेय एतयोरेकं तन्मे ब्रूहि सुनिश्चितम्॥
verses.transliteration:
saṃnyāsaṃ karmaṇāṃ kṛṣṇa punaryogaṃ ca śaṃsasi
yacchreya etayorekaṃ tanme brūhi suniścitam
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: you praise renunciation of actions, Krishna, and again yoga. Which one is better? Tell me decisively.
verses.translation: Renunciation of actions, O Krishna, Thou praisest, and again Yoga. Tell me conclusively that which is the better of the two.

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, accusative singular (agreeing with तत्)
anvaya.parts: सु (well) + निश्चित (determined): 'well determined'

verses.explanation: Arjuna's bookkeeping is fair: chapter 4 ended praising both the renunciation of works (4.41) and the command to rise and act (4.42) in consecutive breaths. He asks his recurring question a third time — which one, decided — still hoping the spiritual life resolves to a single instruction. The persistence is not dullness; it is how a practical man honors a teaching: by demanding it be actionable.
verses.connection: Triggered by the apparent double message of 4.41–42, echoing the 'one thing' demands of 2.7 and 3.2.
verses.reflection: When two goods compete for you, ask a wiser voice the decisive question: which is better for me?
verses.background: Arjuna opens the chapter with his accounting of a contradiction: Krishna has praised renouncing actions and also performing them. He asks for one answer, decided — which of the two is better?
verses.hook: Which is better, renouncing action or acting with devotion?

views.text: Takes the choice as between performing the scriptural rites and giving them up; since one person cannot do both at once, Arjuna wants the single one that brings the good.
Renunciation here means jñāna-yoga. Arjuna asks which of the two, by itself, is superior: easier to practise and quicker in giving the vision of the self.
Arjuna hears a contradiction: renunciation of works was taught for the knower, yet 4.42 says 'take up yoga'; the two cannot belong to one person at one time.
Arjuna is confused because Krishna has praised both renouncing works and working with devotion, which seem opposed, and he wants one clear answer about which is better for him.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
संन्यासः कर्मयोगश्च निःश्रेयसकरावुभौ ।
तयोस्तु कर्मसंन्यासात्कर्मयोगो विशिष्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
saṃnyāsaḥ karmayogaśca niḥśreyasakarāvubhau
tayostu karmasaṃnyāsātkarmayogo viśiṣyate
verses.essence: Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the highest good; but of the two, karma-yoga excels renunciation of action.
verses.translation: Renunciation and the Yoga of action both lead to the highest bliss; but of the two, the Yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + योग (discipline): 'the discipline of action'
निःश्रेयस (highest good, liberation) + कर (making): 'makers of the highest good'

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, ablative singular (than, in a comparison)
anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + संन्यास (renunciation): 'renunciation of action'
कर्म (action) + योग (discipline)

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is distinguished)

verses.explanation: A straight answer, rare and therefore weighty: both roads reach niḥśreyasa — but for *you*, for the embodied beginner, working wins. Not because renunciation is false; because renunciation is an achievement masquerading as a starting point. One cannot resign from what one has not yet stopped craving; karma-yoga is how the craving is actually worked out of the system.
verses.connection: Answers 5.1 cleanly, then spends the chapter showing why the two roads were never really two.
verses.reflection: Choose the engaged path today simply because it is doable from exactly where you stand.
verses.background: Krishna ranks them — both lead to the highest, but karma-yoga excels formal renunciation — and then dissolves the ranking: the true sannyasi is the one beyond cravings and aversions in the midst of work; Sankhya and Yoga are one path seen by the childish as two.
verses.hook: Which path is safer for most people, renouncing work or devoted work?

refs.note: Lakṣmaṇa tells Rāma that Rāma alone is his master and everything, so he needs no worldly duties, expressing the renouncer's attitude.

views.text: Both lead to liberation only because both give rise to knowledge; the karma-yoga that excels is compared with mere renunciation of acts not grounded in knowledge.
Grants that jñāna-yoga and karma-yoga are independent means to the highest good; karma-yoga is still the better of the two, and the next verses say why.
The two are not alternatives: joined together they yield liberation. Yoga ranks higher because without yoga renunciation does not even exist.
Arjuna, still identifying with the body, is told to take up karma-yoga; renunciation comes later, for the purified knower. The two work as successive stages, not rivals.

Renunciation suits souls already beyond body-consciousness, but if the renouncer's mind is not absorbed in God they fall into idleness. Working with devotion is safer for most, since work remains to fall back on.

verses.devanagari:
ज्ञेयः स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ्क्षति ।
निर्द्वन्द्वो हि महाबाहो सुखं बन्धात्प्रमुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
jñeyaḥ sa nityasaṃnyāsī yo na dveṣṭi na kāṅkṣati
nirdvandvo hi mahābāho sukhaṃ bandhātpramucyate
verses.essence: Know as a perpetual renunciate the one who neither hates nor desires; beyond the pairs, Mahabaho, one is easily released from bondage.
verses.translation: He should be known as a perpetual Sannyasi who neither hates nor desires; for, free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed Arjuna, he is easily set free from bondage.

anvaya.form: gerundive, masculine, nominative singular (to be known)

anvaya.parts: नित्य (constant) + संन्यासिन् (renouncer): 'one who always renounces'

anvaya.meaning: free from the pairs of opposites
anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + द्वन्द्व (pair of opposites): 'one without the pairs'
महा (great) + बाहु (arm): 'one whose arms are mighty'

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, accusative singular used as adverb (easily)
verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is released)

verses.explanation: Renunciation gets redefined out of geography: the nitya-sannyāsī is not the one who left home but the one whom craving and aversion have left — possibly while standing in an office, a kitchen, a chariot. The robe is incidental; nirdvandva, freedom from the push-pull pairs, is the substance. By this definition a working Arjuna could renounce more truly than a resentful hermit.
verses.connection: Begins dissolving 5.1's dichotomy: true sannyasa is a state achievable inside karma-yoga itself.
verses.reflection: Be the constant renunciate once today: neither craving the pleasant task nor hating the unpleasant one.
verses.background: Krishna ranks them — both lead to the highest, but karma-yoga excels formal renunciation — and then dissolves the ranking: the true sannyasi is the one beyond cravings and aversions in the midst of work; Sankhya and Yoga are one path seen by the childish as two.
verses.hook: Who counts as a true renunciate even while living an active life?

views.text: This is the karma-yogi: whoever stays without hate or craving amid pleasure, pain and their causes counts as a constant renouncer even while engaged in action.
Content with the experience of the self that karma-yoga already holds, he wants nothing else and so hates nothing; he ranks as one devoted to jñāna-yoga.
Dropping work out of laziness, a family quarrel or unemployment is not sannyasa, and an ochre robe makes no one a renouncer; the pure, desireless heart does.
One who does their duties while inwardly detached, neither hating nor desiring, is a true renunciate. Accepting joy and pain as God's grace lets the world shape us, like a sculptor's chisel.

verses.devanagari:
साङ्ख्ययोगौ पृथग्बालाः प्रवदन्ति न पण्डिताः ।
एकमप्यास्थितः सम्यगुभयोर्विन्दते फलम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sāṅkhyayogau pṛthagbālāḥ pravadanti na paṇḍitāḥ
ekamapyāsthitaḥ samyagubhayorvindate phalam
verses.essence: Children, not the wise, declare Sankhya and Yoga to be different. Established rightly in even one, a person finds the fruit of both.
verses.translation: Children, not the wise, speak of knowledge and the Yoga of action or the performance of action as though they are distinct and different; he who is truly established in one obtains the fruits of both.

anvaya.parts: साङ्ख्य (path of knowledge) + योग (path of action): 'Sankhya and Yoga', a pair

anvaya.base: आ + √स्था · to stand on, resort to

verses.explanation: The verdict on the whole debate: only bālāḥ — children in understanding — see two rival schools where the wise see one mountain with two faces. The operative word is samyak, *rightly*: knowledge truly lived issues in selfless action; selfless action truly practiced ripens into knowledge. Each path, taken to its depth, secretly performs the other.
verses.connection: Elevates 5.2's ranking into reconciliation: the comparison Arjuna keeps requesting rests on a beginner's distinction.
verses.reflection: Stop splitting head and hands; let today's understanding act, and today's actions understand.
verses.background: Krishna ranks them — both lead to the highest, but karma-yoga excels formal renunciation — and then dissolves the ranking: the true sannyasi is the one beyond cravings and aversions in the midst of work; Sankhya and Yoga are one path seen by the childish as two.
verses.hook: Are the paths of knowledge and of action really different destinations?

refs.note: The highest devotee accepts sense objects without craving or aversion, seeing all as God's energy for His service; so outward work and inner renunciation meet.

views.text: 'Sankhya' and 'yoga' are renunciation and karma-yoga once joined with knowledge and its means; their one result is liberation, so the Lord is not leaving Arjuna's question.
It is a child's view that karma-yoga only yields jñāna-yoga while jñāna-yoga alone yields the vision of the self; both have that vision as their common fruit.
Because the two are stages in one sequence, asking which is better, as if they were alternatives, suits only the unwise; either, rightly held, ends in liberation through knowledge.

There are two kinds of renunciation: escapist and unstable, or seeing everything as God's to be used in His service. Karma yogis with the second kind are inwardly equal to renunciants, so both paths bear the same fruit.

verses.devanagari:
यत्साङ्ख्यैः प्राप्यते स्थानं तद्योगैरपि गम्यते ।
एकं साङ्ख्यं च योगं च यः पश्यति स पश्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
yatsāṅkhyaiḥ prāpyate sthānaṃ tadyogairapi gamyate
ekaṃ sāṅkhyaṃ ca yogaṃ ca yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati
verses.essence: The state reached by the Sankhyas is reached also by the Yogis. One who sees Sankhya and Yoga as one — that one truly sees.
verses.translation: That place which is reached by the Sankhyas or the Jnanis is reached by the Yogis (Karma Yogis). He sees, who sees knowledge and the performance of action (Karma Yoga) as one.

anvaya.base: साङ्ख्य · follower of the knowledge path

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is reached)

anvaya.base: योग · here: one who practises yoga

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is gone to)

verses.explanation: The reconciliation sealed with the Gita's favorite construction: yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati — whoever sees this, sees. Not 'sees this too' — sees, period; the unity of the contemplative and active paths is made a touchstone of vision itself. Disputes between renouncers and workers are, by this verse, lovers' quarrels inside one house.
verses.connection: Completes 5.4: same summit certified for both routes — the seeing of their oneness is itself realization.
verses.reflection: Whatever your method, aim at the same summit as every other sincere method — and respect the routes.
verses.background: Krishna ranks them — both lead to the highest, but karma-yoga excels formal renunciation — and then dissolves the ranking: the true sannyasi is the one beyond cravings and aversions in the midst of work; Sankhya and Yoga are one path seen by the childish as two.
verses.hook: Does the renunciant reach a higher goal than the person who works?

refs.note: Teaches that the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation, so the inner state, not outward renunciation, decides the destination.

views.text: Yogis reach liberation too, but by way of the monasticism that follows knowledge; Vedic karma-yoga is called 'yoga' and 'renunciation' only figuratively, because it leads there.
Nothing marks one off as 'the knowledge path' and the other as 'yoga': knowledge is never without yoga, nor yoga without knowledge, so the two are identical.
Renouncers reach freedom directly through hearing, reflection and meditation; selfless workers reach the same state indirectly, through purity of heart and the knowledge that dawns.
What counts in spiritual life is where the mind rests, not outward activity. Because the renunciant and the karma yogi both absorb the mind in God, the wise see them as identical inside.

verses.devanagari:
संन्यासस्तु महाबाहो दुःखमाप्तुमयोगतः ।
योगयुक्तो मुनिर्ब्रह्म नचिरेणाधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
saṃnyāsastu mahābāho duḥkhamāptumayogataḥ
yogayukto munirbrahma nacireṇādhigacchati
verses.essence: But renunciation, Mahabaho, is hard to attain without yoga; the sage harnessed in yoga reaches Brahman before long.
verses.translation: But renunciation, O mighty-armed Arjuna, is hard to attain without Yoga; the Yoga-harmonised sage quickly goes to Brahman.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + बाहु (arm)

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, nominative singular (predicate: is hard)
noun with the suffix -तः (from, for lack of)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + योग (yoga): 'lack of yoga'
योग (yoga) + युक्त (joined): 'one joined with yoga'

verses.explanation: Why karma-yoga was ranked first in 5.2: sequence. Renunciation without the prior scrubbing of selfless work is duḥkham āptum — a misery to attempt — because the untrained mind, deprived of activity, simply churns (the hypocrite of 3.6). Action done as yoga wears the ego smooth; then letting go is not a battle but a ripening, and Brahman arrives na cireṇa, without delay.
verses.connection: Gives the practical reason behind 5.2's preference: yoga is renunciation's prerequisite, not its rival.
verses.reflection: Renunciation without engagement breeds brooding; pair one letting-go today with one act of service.
verses.background: Krishna ranks them — both lead to the highest, but karma-yoga excels formal renunciation — and then dissolves the ranking: the true sannyasi is the one beyond cravings and aversions in the midst of work; Sankhya and Yoga are one path seen by the childish as two.
verses.hook: Why is giving up action so hard without first practising selfless work?

views.text: 'Brahman' here names renunciation in the real sense, steadfastness in knowledge of the supreme Self, citing the Upanishadic line that nyāsa (renunciation) is Brahman.
The karma-yogi, contemplating the self as he works, reaches it soon; one who follows jñāna-yoga alone completes it only with great difficulty and after a long time.
Without a purified mind steadiness in knowledge is impossible, so renunciation taken up first only causes trouble; a vārttika is quoted on careless, quarrelsome renouncers.
Renunciation is tested in the world, not in a cave. By doing one's duty as service to God, the mind is purified and true inner detachment ripens; abandoning duty first leaves the mind impure.

verses.devanagari:
योगयुक्तो विशुद्धात्मा विजितात्मा जितेन्द्रियः ।
सर्वभूतात्मभूतात्मा कुर्वन्नपि न लिप्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yogayukto viśuddhātmā vijitātmā jitendriyaḥ
sarvabhūtātmabhūtātmā kurvannapi na lipyate
verses.essence: Yoked in yoga, purified, self-mastered, senses conquered, one's self become the Self of all beings — even acting, one is not stained.
verses.translation: He who is devoted to the path of action, whose mind is quite pure, who has conquered the self, who has subdued his senses and who realises his Self as the Self in all beings, though acting, is not tainted.

anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + युक्त (joined)
विशुद्ध (purified) + आत्मन् (self, mind): 'one whose mind is purified'
विजित (conquered) + आत्मन् (self, body): 'one who has mastered himself'
जित (conquered) + इन्द्रिय (sense): 'one whose senses are conquered'

anvaya.meaning: whose self is the self of all
anvaya.base: सर्वभूतात्मभूतात्मन् · one with all beings' self
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being) + आत्म (self) + भूत (become) + आत्मन् (self): 'one whose self has become the self of all beings'

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is stained)

verses.explanation: The compounds climb a ladder: purified → self-governed → sense-mastered → and then the leap, sarva-bhūtātma-bhūtātmā, one whose self has become the self of all beings. At that height the question of stain collapses: whom would the action harm, whom exploit, when every party to it is oneself? Non-attachment matures here into something warmer — identification with everything.
verses.connection: Shows where 5.6's yoked sage ends up: action becomes stainless because the boundary it could stain has dissolved.
verses.reflection: Become harmless enough that beings relax around you — pets, children, colleagues are honest meters.
verses.background: Krishna ranks them — both lead to the highest, but karma-yoga excels formal renunciation — and then dissolves the ranking: the true sannyasi is the one beyond cravings and aversions in the midst of work; Sankhya and Yoga are one path seen by the childish as two.
verses.hook: Can a person stay untouched while acting, and what marks such a person?

views.text: 'Self of all beings' means fully illumined: his inmost consciousness is the Self of everything from Brahmā to a clump of grass, so acting to guide the world does not bind him.
His self has become 'like' the self of all: contemplating the self, he finds every self, in gods or men, of one nature, knowledge; differences belong to bodies.
Reads the compounds as a chain of causes: yoga purifies the mind, so the body is mastered, so the senses are won, and then he acts for the world's welfare unbound.

The karma yogi united with God has a purified intellect, a conquered mind and controlled senses, and sees God in all beings. Serving God this way brings realised knowledge, making it no different from renunciation.

verses.devanagari:
नैव किञ्चित्करोमीति युक्तो मन्येत तत्त्ववित् ।
पश्यञ्शृण्वन्स्पृशञ्जिघ्रन्नश्नन्गच्छन्स्वपञ्श्वसन्॥
verses.transliteration:
naiva kiñcitkaromīti yukto manyeta tattvavit
paśyañśṛṇvanspṛśañjighrannaśnangacchansvapañśvasan
verses.essence: 'I do nothing at all' — so should the harnessed knower of truth think, while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing.
verses.translation: "I do nothing at all," thus would the harmonised knower of Truth think seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, going, sleeping, breathing.

anvaya.parts: तत्त्व (truth, reality) + विद् (knower): 'one who knows the truth'

verses.explanation: The inner monologue of the freed, audited against a deliberately mundane list — not battles and sacrifices but smelling, walking, sleeping, breathing. Precisely amid the most automatic acts, the tattva-vit notices: machinery is running; I am the one in whom the running appears. The thought 'naiva kiñcit karomi' is not denial of activity but accurate attribution of it.
verses.connection: Translates 5.7's stainlessness into the texture of an ordinary day — continued into the next verse.
verses.reflection: During one routine act today, note inwardly: seeing happens, hearing happens — I am the witnessing.
verses.background: The technique of the engaged renunciate is given: moving through seeing, hearing, touching while knowing 'the senses move among sense-objects'; acting with body, mind, and intellect with attachment abandoned, offering works to Brahman — stained no more than the lotus leaf by water.
verses.hook: How does the knower of truth regard ordinary acts like seeing and eating?

refs.note: Sage Vasiṣṭha tells Rāma to work diligently outwardly while inwardly seeing himself as the non-doer and God as the mover, the very attitude this verse describes.

views.text: For the knower who sees only inaction in every bodily movement, renouncing all action is the only fitting course, as no one walks to a mirage for water once he knows it is a mirage.
He should reflect that his nature is knowledge; the sense of being the doer comes from the self's tie to senses and life-breaths rooted in karma, not from the self.
The steadfast one here is the karma-yogi who has become a knower of truth step by step; lacking the pride of doership, he is not stained even while doing all these acts.
Pride of doership is a major obstacle. God-conscious karma yogis see themselves as separate from the body and attribute all actions to God's power, considering Him the real doer.

verses.devanagari:
प्रलपन्विसृजन्गृह्णन्नुन्मिषन्निमिषन्नपि ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेषु वर्तन्त इति धारयन्॥
verses.transliteration:
pralapanvisṛjangṛhṇannunmiṣannimiṣannapi
indriyāṇīndriyārtheṣu vartanta iti dhārayan
verses.essence: Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing the eyes — convinced that the senses move among the sense-objects.
verses.translation: Speaking, letting go, seizing, opening and closing the eyes convinced that the senses move among the sense-objects.

anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + अर्थ (object): 'objects of the senses'

anvaya.form: causative present participle, masculine, nominative singular (holding)

verses.explanation: The list reaches its finest grain — even the eyelid's blink — and then gives the formula that reclassifies it all: indriyāṇi indriyārtheṣu vartante, senses operating upon sense-objects, nature transacting with nature (3.28's insight made into a daily mantra). Dhārayan: this is something *held*, a sustained recollection, not a one-time realization.
verses.connection: Completes 5.8's audit and supplies the holding-thought that keeps doership from re-adhering.
verses.reflection: Let the senses meet their objects this hour while you remain the host, not the guest swept along.
verses.background: The technique of the engaged renunciate is given: moving through seeing, hearing, touching while knowing 'the senses move among sense-objects'; acting with body, mind, and intellect with attachment abandoned, offering works to Brahman — stained no more than the lotus leaf by water.
verses.hook: When speaking or blinking, who does the wise person think is acting?

refs.note: Sage Vasiṣṭha tells Rāma to work diligently outwardly while inwardly seeing himself as the non-doer and God as the mover, the very attitude this verse describes.

views.text: The knower of Reality, absorbed in the Self, thinks 'I do nothing' even while seeing, eating or breathing. Seeing inaction in all action, he is fit only to renounce works, as one who knows a mirage holds no water does not go to drink.
He resolves firmly: if eyes and other senses work on their objects, what is that to me? No one is stained by what another does.
Assigns each act to its organ: seeing and the rest to the senses, walking to the feet, sleep to the intellect, breath to prāṇa, speech to the voice, blinking to the kūrma breath.
The sage stays a witness of the senses' activity: the eyes see, the ears hear, but he does not; his actions have been burnt in the fire of wisdom.
Pride of doership is a major obstacle. God-conscious karma yogis see themselves as separate from the body and attribute all actions to God's power, considering Him the real doer.

verses.devanagari:
ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः ।
लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा॥
verses.transliteration:
brahmaṇyādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ
lipyate na sa pāpena padmapatramivāmbhasā
verses.essence: One who acts placing all actions in Brahman, abandoning attachment, is untouched by sin — as a lotus leaf by water.
verses.translation: He who does actions, offering them to Brahman, and abandoning attachment, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus-leaf is not tainted by water.

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is stained)

anvaya.parts: पद्म (lotus) + पत्र (leaf): 'leaf of a lotus'

verses.explanation: The chapter's signature image. The lotus leaf lives on the water — born of it, resting on it, wetted by every rain — yet drops roll off its surface, finding nothing to grip. So the one who acts brahmaṇy ādhāya karmāṇi, placing actions in Brahman and letting attachment go: fully in the world's water, never soaked by it. The leaf does not avoid the pond; its immunity is by surface, not by distance. This is not the dry detachment of withdrawal but a texture of being the world's moisture cannot penetrate — sanctity as a coating, not a quarantine.
verses.connection: Gives 5.7–9 its emblem: stainlessness pictured as the lotus leaf's effortless non-absorption.
verses.reflection: Work soaked in offering today and let blame slide off you as water off a lotus leaf.
verses.background: The technique of the engaged renunciate is given: moving through seeing, hearing, touching while knowing 'the senses move among sense-objects'; acting with body, mind, and intellect with attachment abandoned, offering works to Brahman — stained no more than the lotus leaf by water.
verses.hook: How can someone act in the world and stay free from sin?

views.text: Spoken of one not yet knowing the truth: he gives all actions to God as a servant works for his master, unattached even to liberation, and the sure result is a purified heart.
'Brahman' here means Prakṛti (as in 14.3); seeing that all actions proceed from Prakṛti in the form of the senses, he is free of the sin of taking the body for the self.
Brahman is the Supreme Lord. This verse answers the bind of one who still feels 'I do': unfit to renounce, he offers actions to the Lord and drops attachment to their fruit.
Like a lotus leaf that floats on water yet stays dry, karma yogis remain untouched by sin while doing all kinds of work, because they act in divine consciousness.

verses.devanagari:
कायेन मनसा बुद्ध्या केवलैरिन्द्रियैरपि ।
योगिनः कर्म कुर्वन्ति सङ्गं त्यक्त्वात्मशुद्धये॥
verses.transliteration:
kāyena manasā buddhyā kevalairindriyairapi
yoginaḥ karma kurvanti saṅgaṃ tyaktvātmaśuddhaye
verses.essence: With body, mind, understanding, or even the senses alone, yogis perform action — abandoning attachment, for self-purification.
verses.translation: Yogis, having abandoned attachment, perform actions only by the body, mind, intellect, and even by the senses, for the purification of the self.

anvaya.parts: आत्म (self) + शुद्धि (purification): 'purification of the self'

verses.explanation: The motive of the working sage finally named in full: ātma-śuddhaye, for self-purification. Not for wages, fame, or even merit — action used as soap, each task scrubbing the instrument that performs it. Kevalaiḥ, 'merely', qualifies body, mind, intellect and senses alike: the faculties go on working, but the claim of 'mine' has been taken out of them. What consecrates the work is not its grandeur but that dropped claim of ownership, and the purifying aim it serves.
verses.connection: Answers the lingering 'why act at all?' for 5.10's lotus-leaf yogi: the work is the bath.
verses.reflection: Use body, mind, and intellect today as cleaning tools — every unattached act scrubbing the instrument.
verses.background: The technique of the engaged renunciate is given: moving through seeing, hearing, touching while knowing 'the senses move among sense-objects'; acting with body, mind, and intellect with attachment abandoned, offering works to Brahman — stained no more than the lotus leaf by water.
verses.hook: Why do yogis keep working once they have dropped attachment?

refs.note: Rāma tells Sugrīva he could destroy all demons with a finger; the army exists only to give devotees a chance to serve and be purified.

views.text: 'Merely' goes with body, mind, intellect and senses alike, removing all sense of ownership: 'I act only for God, not for my gain.' Self-purification means purifying the heart.
Giving up desire for heaven and the like, they act to purify the self, which here means cancelling the bonds of past karma that keep the self in saṃsāra.
Spells out the work: with the body, bathing and the like; with the intellect, settling the truth; with senses free of obsession, hearing and chanting the Lord's praise.

God needs nothing from us; the one thing we can offer Him is a purified heart. Enlightened yogis therefore work to purify themselves for His pleasure, even welcoming hardship as a chance to grow purer.

verses.devanagari:
युक्तः कर्मफलं त्यक्त्वा शान्तिमाप्नोति नैष्ठिकीम् ।
अयुक्तः कामकारेण फले सक्तो निबध्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yuktaḥ karmaphalaṃ tyaktvā śāntimāpnoti naiṣṭhikīm
ayuktaḥ kāmakāreṇa phale sakto nibadhyate
verses.essence: The harnessed one, abandoning the fruit of action, attains lasting peace; the unharnessed, attached to fruit by desire's prompting, is bound.
verses.translation: The united one (the well poised or the harmonised) having abandoned the fruit of action attains to the eternal peace: the non-united only (the unsteady or the unbalanced) impelled by desire, attached to the fruit, is bound.

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + फल (fruit): 'fruit of action'
अ (not) + युक्त (joined): 'one not joined in yoga'
काम (desire) + कार (doing, impulse): 'action prompted by desire'

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is bound)

verses.explanation: The fork drawn in one couplet: same work, two inner contracts. One signs away the fruit and receives śāntim naiṣṭhikīm — peace with a foundation, peace that stays; the other, kāma-kāreṇa, under desire's compulsion, clutches the fruit and finds the clutch is a shackle. The fruit was never the prize or the problem; the grip is both.
verses.connection: Compresses the chapter's economics: 5.11's purifying work versus its desire-driven double.
verses.reflection: Trade one outcome-anxiety today for the steady peace of work well surrendered.
verses.background: The technique of the engaged renunciate is given: moving through seeing, hearing, touching while knowing 'the senses move among sense-objects'; acting with body, mind, and intellect with attachment abandoned, offering works to Brahman — stained no more than the lotus leaf by water.
verses.hook: Why does the same action bind one person but free another?

views.text: 'Yukta' is one resolved that actions are for God, not for his gain. The peace is liberation, reached in stages: a purified heart, knowledge, renunciation of all action, steadfastness in knowledge.
The yogi wants no fruit but the self, and his lasting peace is the steady experience of the self; the unsteady one, turned toward other fruits, stays bound in saṃsāra.
The same action frees one person and binds another: the one devoted solely to the Supreme Lord gains final peace, while one turned outward, driven by desire, is bound.
Those united with God who want no reward but purification attain lasting peace, while those craving material results become bound by the reactions of their work.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वकर्माणि मनसा संन्यस्यास्ते सुखं वशी ।
नवद्वारे पुरे देही नैव कुर्वन्न कारयन्॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvakarmāṇi manasā saṃnyasyāste sukhaṃ vaśī
navadvāre pure dehī naiva kurvanna kārayan
verses.essence: Mentally renouncing all actions, the embodied one sits happily, master in the nine-gated city — neither acting nor causing action.
verses.translation: Mentally renouncing all actions and self-controlled, the embodied one rests happily in the nine-gated city, neither acting nor causing others (body and senses) to act.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + कर्मन् (action): 'all actions'

anvaya.base: सम् + नि + √अस् · to lay down, renounce

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, accusative singular used as adverb (happily)
adjective, neuter, locative singular (in), agreeing with पुरे
anvaya.parts: नव (nine) + द्वार (gate): 'that which has nine gates'

anvaya.base: देहिन् · one who has a body

anvaya.form: causative present participle, masculine, nominative singular (making others act)

verses.explanation: The body re-imagined as architecture: nava-dvāre pure, the city of nine gates — eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth and the rest — with the Self as resident sovereign, not as gatekeeper, porter or merchant. The gates stay open; traffic flows; the king āste sukham, sits at ease, having mentally signed the whole municipality over to nature. Renunciation, again, is an address change within, not a change of address.
verses.connection: The interior view of 5.10's lotus leaf: how non-absorption feels from inside the body it inhabits.
verses.reflection: Rest once today as the ruler of the nine-gated city — present in it, governed by none of its gates.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord who takes on no one's sin or merit; wisdom rising like a sun once ignorance is destroyed; the even-seeing sages who conquer rebirth here itself; joy turned inward and found unending.
verses.hook: What does it mean to live in the body without being its doer?

refs.note: Describes the body as a city of nine gates in which the soul dwells alongside the Lord; linked with the Lord, the soul is free while embodied.

views.text: Only one who knows the Self as distinct from body and senses can say 'I am in the body, as in a house'; the ignorant say 'I am on the seat'. He remains there while past karma runs out.
He assigns all actions to the body of nine openings, seeing that they arise from the self's link with a body rooted in past karma, not from the self's own nature.
Now, for the pure-minded, renunciation is best. Free of 'I', he does not act; free of 'mine', he does not make others act, unlike the impure renouncer who starts acting again.
The body is a city of nine gates with the soul as its king. Enlightened yogis regard the body and its actions as belonging to God and live happily as detached witnesses.

verses.devanagari:
न कर्तृत्वं न कर्माणि लोकस्य सृजति प्रभुः ।
न कर्मफलसंयोगं स्वभावस्तु प्रवर्तते॥
verses.transliteration:
na kartṛtvaṃ na karmāṇi lokasya sṛjati prabhuḥ
na karmaphalasaṃyogaṃ svabhāvastu pravartate
verses.essence: The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the union of action with fruit; it is nature that operates.
verses.translation: Neither agency nor actions does the Lord create for the world, nor union with the fruits of actions. But it is Nature that acts.

anvaya.base: कर्तृत्व · the state of being a doer

anvaya.meaning: the link of action with fruit
anvaya.base: कर्मफलसंयोग · union with fruits of action
anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + फल (fruit) + संयोग (union): 'union with the fruit of action'
स्व (own) + भाव (being, nature): 'one's own nature'

anvaya.base: प्र + √वृत् · to set in motion, proceed

verses.explanation: A theological boundary, drawn with surprising restraint: the prabhu does not micro-author doership, deeds, or even the action-fruit linkage — svabhāva, the inherent nature of things, runs the machinery. The verse protects two things at once: divine purity from the world's crimes, and human responsibility from the excuse 'God made me do it.' The system is His; the steering, within it, is ours.
verses.connection: Widens 5.13's inner kingship to cosmology: even the supreme Resident does not turn the gears directly.
verses.reflection: Stop blaming the Lord of the city for the city's traffic; nature runs the machinery you resent.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord who takes on no one's sin or merit; wisdom rising like a sun once ignorance is destroyed; the even-seeing sages who conquer rebirth here itself; joy turned inward and found unending.
verses.hook: Does God decide our actions and make us feel we are the doers?

views.text: Prabhu is the Self, which gives no one the command 'do this'. The svabhāva that acts is ignorance, the Māyā spoken of in 7.14.
Prabhu is the individual self, master of the body; agency and the rest come from vāsanās born of Prakṛti through beginningless karma, not from the self's pure nature.
The Lord is Conscious Energy whose very nature puts forth creation, maintenance and withdrawal; there is no separate creatorhood, action or fruit apart from It.
Prabhu is Īśvara. Answering the charge of partiality and cruelty, it is the jīva's own beginningless ignorance that takes the form of doership; the Lord only directs beings by it.

God is not the director of our deeds nor the source of our pride of doership; the soul takes that on through ignorance. Giving up doership is the soul's own responsibility, which God's grace then helps.

verses.devanagari:
नादत्ते कस्यचित्पापं न चैव सुकृतं विभुः ।
अज्ञानेनावृतं ज्ञानं तेन मुह्यन्ति जन्तवः॥
verses.transliteration:
nādatte kasyacitpāpaṃ na caiva sukṛtaṃ vibhuḥ
ajñānenāvṛtaṃ jñānaṃ tena muhyanti jantavaḥ
verses.essence: The all-pervading takes on no one's sin nor anyone's merit. Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby creatures are deluded.
verses.translation: The Lord takes neither the demerit nor even the merit of any; knowledge is enveloped by ignorance, thereby beings are deluded.

anvaya.parts: सु (well) + कृत (done): 'what is well done'

verses.explanation: The Lord keeps no ledger of credits and debts to dispense by whim — the vibhu neither absorbs our sins nor banks our virtues; karma is self-executing law, not divine bookkeeping. Then the real culprit behind all suffering is arraigned in three words: ajñānena āvṛtaṁ jñānam — knowing, veiled by unknowing. Not wickedness at the root of the world's pain, but a covering.
verses.connection: Completes 5.14's separation of God from the machinery — and names the veil the next verse will burn.
verses.reflection: Withdraw one judgment today, remembering: the sun of awareness takes neither credit nor sin.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord who takes on no one's sin or merit; wisdom rising like a sun once ignorance is destroyed; the even-seeing sages who conquer rebirth here itself; joy turned inward and found unending.
verses.hook: Is God responsible for our good and bad deeds?

views.text: The all-pervading accepts no one's sin, not even a devotee's, and no one's virtue. Deluded by covered knowledge, people think 'I act, I make others act, I eat, I make others eat.'
Vibhu is the self, not confined to any body and no one's relative or enemy. Its knowledge is contracted by past karma, which produces the error of taking bodies for selves.
The Lord is wholly fulfilled and wants nothing, so He takes on no merit or sin; even His punishment is grace, and only ignorance makes people think Him partial.
God supplies the power to act, notes our deeds and gives results, like an umpire. The soul has free will, which makes love possible, so our deeds are our own and not God's fault.

verses.devanagari:
ज्ञानेन तु तदज्ञानं येषां नाशितमात्मनः ।
तेषामादित्यवज्ज्ञानं प्रकाशयति तत्परम्॥
verses.transliteration:
jñānena tu tadajñānaṃ yeṣāṃ nāśitamātmanaḥ
teṣāmādityavajjñānaṃ prakāśayati tatparam
verses.essence: But for those whose ignorance is destroyed by Self-knowledge, that knowledge, like the sun, illumines the Supreme.
verses.translation: But to those whose ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge of the Self, like the sun, knowledge reveals the Supreme (Brahman).

anvaya.form: causative past participle, neuter, nominative singular (destroyed)

anvaya.parts: आदित्य (sun) + वत् (like): 'as the sun does'

verses.explanation: The counter-verse: when the veil of 5.15 is burned, what remains is ādityavat — sunlike. The simile is chosen for its manner of working: the sun does not argue the darkness away or defeat it piece by piece; it rises, and darkness is simply not there. So Self-knowledge does not refute delusion — it outshines the conditions under which delusion was possible.
verses.connection: Answers 5.15's veil with its solvent: knowledge as sunrise, after which the Supreme is self-evident.
verses.reflection: Let one insight today rise like sunrise — not adding light to the Self, just removing a cloud.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord who takes on no one's sin or merit; wisdom rising like a sun once ignorance is destroyed; the even-seeing sages who conquer rebirth here itself; joy turned inward and found unending.
verses.hook: What happens to ignorance once true knowledge dawns?

refs.note: Says the moon and all the stars together cannot end the night, but the sunrise does at once; so too God's knowledge dispels ignorance.

views.text: Ignorance, which covers and deludes beings, is destroyed by discriminating knowledge of the Self; that knowledge then reveals the supreme Reality, the highest Goal, as the sun reveals all forms.
'For those' shows selves remain many even after ignorance is gone. Knowledge is an attribute of the self, like the sun's light: contracted by karma in saṃsāra, it expands in release.
Once illusion is destroyed, knowledge's natural power to light itself and all else simply starts working, as the sun shines when darkness goes or nectar acts once the doubt of poison is gone.
Knowledge of the Lord removes the false notion that He is partial, and then reveals Īśvara in His fullness, as the sun drives off darkness and shows every object.
Just as the sun instantly ends the night, the light of God's knowledge dispels the illusion of being the body and the doer, waking the soul to its spiritual identity.

verses.devanagari:
तद्बुद्धयस्तदात्मानस्तन्निष्ठास्तत्परायणाः ।
गच्छन्त्यपुनरावृत्तिं ज्ञाननिर्धूतकल्मषाः॥
verses.transliteration:
tadbuddhayastadātmānastanniṣṭhāstatparāyaṇāḥ
gacchantyapunarāvṛttiṃ jñānanirdhūtakalmaṣāḥ
verses.essence: Their understanding in That, their self in That, established in That, devoted to That — they go to the state of no return, their stains shaken off by knowledge.
verses.translation: Their intellect absorbed in That, their self being That, established in That, with That for their supreme goal, they go whence there is no return, their sins dispelled by knowledge.

anvaya.base: तद्बुद्धि · whose intellect is in That
anvaya.parts: तद् (That) + बुद्धि (intellect): 'those whose intellect rests in That'
तद् (That) + आत्मन् (self, mind): 'those whose self is That'
तद् (That) + निष्ठा (steadfastness): 'those steadfast in That'
तद् (That) + परायण (highest goal, refuge): 'those whose supreme refuge is That'
अ (not) + पुनर् (again) + आवृत्ति (return): 'not coming back again'

anvaya.meaning: their stains shaken off by knowledge
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + निर्धूत (shaken off) + कल्मष (stain, sin): 'those whose stains are shaken off by knowledge'

verses.explanation: Four times tat, That — understanding, identity, foundation, final refuge, all relocated into the one Reality, the way a compass needle gives the north every fiber of its attention. The result is the tradition's strongest word for finality: apunar-āvṛtti, no return — not a higher rung on the wheel but the wheel's exit. Nirdhūta: the stains are not scrubbed but *shaken off*, as a bird shakes water.
verses.connection: Traces the trajectory of 5.16's sunrise to its terminus: total orientation, total release.
verses.reflection: Point intellect, mind, conviction, and refuge at one thing today, and feel the four engines align.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord who takes on no one's sin or merit; wisdom rising like a sun once ignorance is destroyed; the even-seeing sages who conquer rebirth here itself; joy turned inward and found unending.
verses.hook: What becomes of those whose whole mind and goal rest in the Supreme?

views.text: They have the supreme Brahman itself as their Self and stand in it alone, having renounced all action; non-return means never again being joined to a body.
'That' is the individual self they resolve to see and meditate on; the state of no return is the self resting in its own nature.
Describes the fruit of worshipping the Lord: with intellect, mind and refuge in Him, their stains are removed by self-knowledge gained through His grace, and they reach liberation.
Knowledge that frees from rebirth comes with devotion. The verse's terms describe an intellect, heart, faith and striving wholly fixed on God, and true knowledge shows itself as love for Him.

verses.devanagari:
विद्याविनयसम्पन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि ।
शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः॥
verses.transliteration:
vidyāvinayasampanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini
śuni caiva śvapāke ca paṇḍitāḥ samadarśinaḥ
verses.essence: In a brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an eater of dogs — the wise see the same.
verses.translation: Sages look with an equal eye on a Brahmana endowed with learning and humility, on a cow, on an elephant, and even on a dog and an outcaste.

anvaya.base: विद्याविनयसम्पन्न · rich in learning and modesty
anvaya.parts: विद्या (learning) + विनय (humility) + सम्पन्न (endowed): 'one endowed with learning and humility'

anvaya.base: श्वपाक · one who cooks dogs, outcaste
anvaya.parts: श्व (dog) + पाक (cooking): 'one who cooks dogs'
सम (same, equal) + दर्शिन् (seer): 'those who see the same'

verses.explanation: The vision of 5.16–17 tested against the steepest social gradient its world knew: from the cultured brahmin through revered, mighty, and despised animals to the śvapāka, the outcaste his society placed beneath them all. The paṇḍita's eye registers the differences of form and finds, beneath every one, the identical resident. Commentators are careful: sama-darśana is equal seeing of the indwelling Self, not identical treatment of every role — the wise look on all equally; they do not act toward all identically. Yet the gaze, once true, leaves no room for contempt: hierarchy may remain at the surface, but at the root it is abolished.
verses.connection: The social proof of knowledge: 5.17's That-absorbed seer, turned outward, sees one Self wearing every rank.
verses.reflection: Practice the level gaze once: see the same consciousness in the scholar, the animal, the outcast.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord who takes on no one's sin or merit; wisdom rising like a sun once ignorance is destroyed; the even-seeing sages who conquer rebirth here itself; joy turned inward and found unending.
verses.hook: How do the wise see a scholar, a cow, a dog and an outcaste?

views.text: They see one unchanging Brahman, untouched by the guṇas, in the sattvic brahmin, the rajasic cow and the tamasic elephant and dog alike.
The selves are many but all share one form, knowledge; the striking differences among brahmin, cow, dog and outcaste belong to Prakṛti, the body, not to the self.
They hold no notion of gaining merit by serving the brahmin or of impurity in the dog; the verse says they look on all equally, not that they act toward all identically.
The list shows two kinds of inequality: by conduct, the learned brahmin and the dog-cooker; by species, the cow, elephant and dog. The wise see the same Brahman in both kinds.
Divine knowledge comes with humility and sees all beings as souls, fragments of God, so the learned regard everyone equally. Caste does not make anyone higher or lower.

verses.devanagari:
इहैव तैर्जितः सर्गो येषां साम्ये स्थितं मनः ।
निर्दोषं हि समं ब्रह्म तस्माद् ब्रह्मणि ते स्थिताः॥
verses.transliteration:
ihaiva tairjitaḥ sargo yeṣāṃ sāmye sthitaṃ manaḥ
nirdoṣaṃ hi samaṃ brahma tasmād brahmaṇi te sthitāḥ
verses.essence: Even here, birth is conquered by those whose mind rests in sameness; flawless and the same is Brahman — therefore they stand in Brahman.
verses.translation: Even here (in this world) birth (everything) is overcome by those whose minds rest in equality; Brahman is spotless indeed and equal; therefore they are established in Brahman.

anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + दोष (fault): 'without fault'

verses.explanation: The logic of sameness made explicit, and it runs like a proof: Brahman's two properties are nirdoṣa and sama — flawless, equal everywhere; therefore a mind that has become genuinely equal has taken on Brahman's own signature and must already be standing in it. And the timestamp: iha eva, *here itself* — the conquest of rebirth is verified in this life, by the evenness of this mind.
verses.connection: Converts 5.18's equal vision from ethics into metaphysics: sameness of sight is residence in Brahman, now.
verses.reflection: Win a little of that freedom here today: meet one unequal situation with a perfectly equal mind.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord who takes on no one's sin or merit; wisdom rising like a sun once ignorance is destroyed; the even-seeing sages who conquer rebirth here itself; joy turned inward and found unending.
verses.hook: Can someone overcome the cycle of birth while still living here?

refs.note: Lakṣmaṇa served Rāma and Sītā as naturally as an ignorant man serves his body, showing a mind fully absorbed in God.
One who desires nothing becomes fit to be like Brahman, linking freedom from desire with the equanimity this verse praises.

views.text: Brahman dwells even in the dog-eater yet stays untouched by any defect, and has no qualities or ultimate distinctions to divide it; standing in it, they too are touched by no fault.
Saṃsāra is overcome even while still practising the means. 'Brahman' here is the self, the same everywhere once free of Prakṛti; abiding in that sameness is the conquest.
Answers the objection from Gautama's law, which faults honouring unequals equally: that fault applies only before one reaches Brahman; those who see the same have already attained it.

Equal vision means rising above likes and dislikes, pleasure and pain. This is impossible while identified with the body; saints who absorb the mind in God transcend these dualities and become godlike.

verses.devanagari:
न प्रहृष्येत्प्रियं प्राप्य नोद्विजेत्प्राप्य चाप्रियम् ।
स्थिरबुद्धिरसम्मूढो ब्रह्मविद् ब्रह्मणि स्थितः॥
verses.transliteration:
na prahṛṣyetpriyaṃ prāpya nodvijetprāpya cāpriyam
sthirabuddhirasammūḍho brahmavid brahmaṇi sthitaḥ
verses.essence: One should not rejoice on gaining the pleasant nor shudder on meeting the unpleasant — steady-minded, undeluded, the knower of Brahman stands in Brahman.
verses.translation: Resting in Brahman, with steady intellect and undeluded, the knower of Brahman neither rejoiceth on obtaining what is pleasant nor grieveth on obtaining what is unpleasant.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, accusative singular (object)
adjective used as noun, neuter, accusative singular (object)

anvaya.parts: स्थिर (steady) + बुद्धि (intellect): one whose intellect is steady

anvaya.form: past participle with negation, masculine, nominative singular (subject)

anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Brahman) + विद् (knowing): one who knows Brahman

verses.explanation: The daily examination for 5.19's claim: priya arrives — no leap; apriya arrives — no lurch. Not numbness, but the absence of the two convulsions by which events normally seize the steering. Each unshaken meeting with the pleasant and unpleasant is a small certification, renewed in real time, that one's standing is in Brahman and not in the weather.
verses.connection: Brings the Brahman-standing of 5.19 to street level: equanimity as its hourly evidence.
verses.reflection: Receive one pleasant thing and one unpleasant thing today with the same inner temperature.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord untainted as sky; wisdom rising like a sun on the Self; the even-seeing sages for whom heaven is already won; joy turned inward and found unending.

views.text: Steady intellect means unwavering conviction that one taintless Self dwells in all beings. Gain and loss cause joy and sorrow only for one who takes the body as the Self; for the realized there is nothing to gain or lose.

Pleasant and unpleasant experiences arise from old karmic impressions and belong to Prakṛti, so they are transient. The mind stays fixed on the steadfast self, free from confusing it with the body, learned through teachers' instruction.
For one who sees all alike, the division into friends and foes remains only at the level of worldly dealings, never inwardly, because he is firmly established in Brahman.
Neither rejoicing in pleasure nor grieving over pain comes naturally through devotion: when one's will merges with God's will, every outcome is accepted serenely as His grace.

verses.hook: How does someone established in the Supreme react to good and bad news?

verses.devanagari:
बाह्यस्पर्शेष्वसक्तात्मा विन्दत्यात्मनि यत्सुखम् ।
स ब्रह्मयोगयुक्तात्मा सुखमक्षयमश्नुते॥
verses.transliteration:
bāhyasparśeṣvasaktātmā vindatyātmani yatsukham
sa brahmayogayuktātmā sukhamakṣayamaśnute
verses.essence: With self unattached to outer contacts, one finds the happiness that is in the Self; with self yoked to Brahman by yoga, one enjoys undecaying happiness.
verses.translation: With the self unattached to external contacts he finds happiness in the Self; with the self engaged in the meditation of Brahman he attains to the endless happiness.

anvaya.parts: बाह्य (external) + स्पर्श (contact, object touched): the outer objects of the senses
असक्त (unattached) + आत्मन् (mind, self): one whose mind is unattached

anvaya.meaning: whose self is joined to Brahman by yoga
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Brahman) + योग (yoga, meditation) + युक्त (joined) + आत्मन् (self): one whose self is absorbed in meditation on Brahman

anvaya.form: verb, present, 3rd person singular, middle voice

verses.explanation: The economics of joy, stated as a discovery rather than a sacrifice: loosen the grip on bāhya-sparśa, the outer touches, and a happiness already resident in the Self becomes findable — vindati, one *finds* it, like a coin that was always in the pocket. Its grade is then named: akṣaya, non-depleting. Outer pleasures are drawn from a draining tank; this one from a spring.
verses.connection: Begins the chapter's closing meditation on pleasure (5.21–23): what the equanimous one of 5.20 gets instead.
verses.reflection: Find the joy that needs no object for five minutes — close the doors and discover the house lit.
verses.background: From the chariot Krishna paints the inner sovereign: the embodied one resting happily in the nine-gated city, neither doing nor causing; the Lord untainted as sky; wisdom rising like a sun on the Self; the even-seeing sages for whom heaven is already won; joy turned inward and found unending.

views.text: Brahma-yoga is meditation on Brahman. Whoever wants undecaying happiness in the Self must withdraw the senses from the momentary happiness of outer objects.
Brahman here means the individual self (ātman): leaving contemplation of Prakṛti, the mind dwells on the self, and the lasting bliss is the experience of that self.
The happiness first found within is a calm, sāttvic peace; having gained it, one becomes one with Brahman through samādhi and then reaches imperishable joy.
Scriptures describe God as an ocean of bliss. The yogi who withdraws from outer contacts and absorbs senses, mind and intellect in God begins to taste the infinite bliss of the God within.

verses.hook: Where does a person find happiness that never runs out?

refs.note: Declares that Brahman is bliss, so the endless happiness the verse promises is God's own nature.
Describes the Supreme Lord as a form of pure bliss known by experience.
Says God's hands, feet, face and every part are made of bliss.

verses.devanagari:
ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते ।
आद्यन्तवन्तः कौन्तेय न तेषु रमते बुधः॥
verses.transliteration:
ye hi saṃsparśajā bhogā duḥkhayonaya eva te
ādyantavantaḥ kaunteya na teṣu ramate budhaḥ
verses.essence: The enjoyments born of contact are wombs of sorrow, with beginning and end, Kaunteya; the wise one does not delight in them.
verses.translation: The enjoyments that are born of contacts are only generators of pain, for they have a beginning and an end, O Arjuna; the wise man does not rejoice in them.

anvaya.parts: संस्पर्श (contact of sense and object) + ज (born): arising from contact
दुःख (sorrow) + योनि (womb, source): things whose source-role is sorrow

anvaya.base: आद्यन्तवत् · having a start and an end
anvaya.parts: आदि (beginning) + अन्त (end) + वत् (having): possessing beginning and end

anvaya.form: verb, present, 3rd person singular, middle voice

verses.explanation: A clinical audit of ordinary pleasure: saṁsparśa-ja, contact-born — requiring the meeting of sense and object, hence hostage to both; ādy-antavantaḥ, bracketed by a start and a stop, hence pre-loaded with the ache of ending; therefore duḥkha-yonayaḥ, wombs already pregnant with sorrow. The budha does not flee them in horror — na teṣu ramate, he simply does not *settle* in them, the way one enjoys an inn without mistaking it for home.
verses.connection: The ledger's other column after 5.21: why outer delight, examined, fails the test the inner one passes.
verses.reflection: Audit one favorite pleasure honestly: where it begins, where it ends, and what it leaves.
verses.background: The teaching presses the urgency of here and now: sense-born pleasures are wombs of pain with beginnings and ends; the real strength is withstanding desire and anger before leaving the body; for the self-controlled seer, the bliss of Brahman lies close on every side.

views.text: Such enjoyments are sources of sorrow because they are products of ignorance; eva implies the same holds in other worlds too. Delight in objects is seen only in the very foolish, like animals.
They last only briefly and the reaction after they end is painful. The wise one, who knows himself as ātman, finds no pleasure in them.
Even while present these pleasures are shot through with rivalry and envy, so they are sources of sorrow now, not only when they end.

Worldly pleasures are finite, temporary and steadily diminishing, so they cannot satisfy the soul. God's bliss is infinite, eternal and ever-fresh, and once tasted it makes material pleasure lose its appeal.

verses.hook: Why does the wise person not delight in pleasures of the senses?

verses.devanagari:
शक्नोतीहैव यः सोढुं प्राक्शरीरविमोक्षणात् ।
कामक्रोधोद्भवं वेगं स युक्तः स सुखी नरः॥
verses.transliteration:
śaknotīhaiva yaḥ soḍhuṃ prākśarīravimokṣaṇāt
kāmakrodhodbhavaṃ vegaṃ sa yuktaḥ sa sukhī naraḥ
verses.essence: One who can withstand, here itself before release from the body, the surge born of desire and anger — that one is yoked, that one is a happy person.
verses.translation: He who is able, while still here (in this world) to withstand, before the liberation from the body, the impulse born out of desire and anger he is a Yogi, he is a happy man.

anvaya.parts: शरीर (body) + विमोक्षण (release): the release from the body

anvaya.base: कामक्रोधोद्भव · arising from desire and anger
anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + क्रोध (anger) + उद्भव (origin): that whose origin is desire and anger

verses.explanation: The word vega — surge, flood-force — concedes the enemy's power: desire and anger arrive not as suggestions but as breakers. The test is soḍhum, to withstand the wave without being carried off. And it is set ihaiva, here in this very life, prāk śarīra-vimokṣaṇāt, until the body is let go: as long as one lives, these surges keep rising, so the watch is never relaxed before the end. The verse then collapses two words usually held apart, yukta and sukhī — the disciplined one *is* the happy one. Liberation's evidence is asked for in the present tense.
verses.connection: The fitness test underlying 5.21–22's exchange: inner happiness belongs to whoever can stand in the surf.
verses.reflection: Hold one surge of desire or anger until it passes through you unacted — that is strength, here, now.
verses.background: The teaching presses the urgency of here and now: sense-born pleasures are wombs of pain with beginnings and ends; the real strength is withstanding desire and anger before leaving the body; for the self-controlled seer, the bliss of Brahman lies close on every side.

views.text: Death is named as the limit because the impulse of desire and anger keeps arising, from endless sources, as long as one lives; so one must never relax vigilance until the end.
While still practising, one gains the capacity to experience the self, but full immersion in its bliss comes only after the body falls; there is no complete liberation while embodied.
As a corpse feels nothing when embraced by mourners or burned on the pyre, so one who bears the surge of desire and anger that way while still alive is truly yoked and happy.
The human body uniquely has discrimination. Desire and anger should be withstood not out of fear or shame, but by knowing sense pleasures bring misery; one who does this while alive is a happy yogi.

verses.hook: Who is truly happy, according to this verse?

refs.note: The human body is not for toiling after sense pleasures that even hogs get, but for austerity that purifies the heart and gives God's endless bliss.

verses.devanagari:
योऽन्तःसुखोऽन्तरारामस्तथान्तर्ज्योतिरेव यः ।
स योगी ब्रह्मनिर्वाणं ब्रह्मभूतोऽधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
yo'ntaḥsukho'ntarārāmastathāntarjyotireva yaḥ
sa yogī brahmanirvāṇaṃ brahmabhūto'dhigacchati
verses.essence: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, whose light is within — that yogi, become Brahman, attains the nirvana of Brahman.
verses.translation: He who is happy within, who rejoices within, and who is illuminated within, that Yogi attains absolute freedom or Moksha, himself becoming Brahman.

anvaya.parts: अन्तः (within) + सुख (happiness): one whose happiness is within
अन्तर् (within) + आराम (delight, pleasure-garden): one whose play is within
अन्तर् (within) + ज्योतिस् (light): one whose light is within
ब्रह्म (Brahman) + निर्वाण (blowing out, peace): the stillness that is Brahman
ब्रह्म (Brahman) + भूत (become): one who has become Brahman

verses.explanation: Three relocations complete the move: antaḥ-sukha, antar-ārāma, antar-jyotiḥ — happiness, recreation, and even illumination, all running on inner mains, the house finally off the grid of circumstance. Then the chapter's destination-word arrives: brahma-nirvāṇa, extinction *into* Brahman — not the snuffing of the person but of the person's fever, the lamp losing its flicker by merging with daylight. Brahma-bhūta: not reaching Brahman like a place, but having become what one reaches.
verses.connection: Gathers 5.21–23 into arrival: the withstander's inward turn completes as identity with the goal.
verses.reflection: Locate your happiness indoors today: inner light, inner delight, inner play.
verses.background: The teaching presses the urgency of here and now: sense-born pleasures are wombs of pain with beginnings and ends; the real strength is withstanding desire and anger before leaving the body; for the self-controlled seer, the bliss of Brahman lies close on every side.

views.text: Antar-jyotiḥ means the inner Self alone is his light, so he need not depend on the senses for knowing. Having become Brahman while still living, he attains liberation.
Brahman here is the self: the yogi's joy, pleasure-garden and knowledge are all directed to the self, whose own qualities like bliss and sinlessness increase his happiness.
His happiness, delight and lustre are within and depend on nothing outside; in worldly dealings he may even look ignorant, wandering like a fool with no taste for debate.

Outer temptations can be resisted permanently only when one tastes happiness within. When God's bliss flows in the heart by His grace, fleeting external pleasures seem trivial and are easy to give up.

verses.hook: What lets a person resist outer temptation for good?

refs.note: In samādhi the intellect becomes filled with truth, the inner light the verse speaks of.

verses.devanagari:
लभन्ते ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृषयः क्षीणकल्मषाः ।
छिन्नद्वैधा यतात्मानः सर्वभूतहिते रताः॥
verses.transliteration:
labhante brahmanirvāṇamṛṣayaḥ kṣīṇakalmaṣāḥ
chinnadvaidhā yatātmānaḥ sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ
verses.essence: The seers whose sins are worn away, whose doubts are severed, who are self-restrained and delight in the welfare of all beings — they attain the nirvana of Brahman.
verses.translation: The sages (Rishis) obtain absolute freedom or Moksha they whose sins have been destroyed, whose dualities (perception of dualities or experience of the pairs of opposites) are torn asunder, who are self-controlled, and intent on the welfare of all beings.

anvaya.form: verb, present, 3rd person plural, middle voice

anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Brahman) + निर्वाण (blowing out, peace): the stillness that is Brahman

anvaya.base: क्षीणकल्मष · one whose sins are destroyed
anvaya.parts: क्षीण (worn away) + कल्मष (stain, sin): those whose stains are worn away
छिन्न (cut) + द्वैध (doubleness: doubt, duality): those whose doubleness is cut
यत (restrained) + आत्मन् (mind, self): those whose mind is restrained

anvaya.meaning: in the welfare of all beings
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being) + हित (welfare): the welfare of all beings

verses.explanation: Lest 5.24's inwardness sound like withdrawal, the freed seer's outer life is shown: sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ — *delighting*, ratāḥ, in the good of all beings. Compassion here is not a duty appended to liberation but its overflow: when the boundary between self and others thins (5.7), their welfare becomes one's recreation. The liberated do not leave the world; they finally become safe for it, and useful to it.
verses.connection: Corrects any misreading of 5.24: the inward-lit yogi faces outward in universal benevolence.
verses.reflection: Pair your inner work with outer kindness today — the rishis kept both hands open.
verses.background: The teaching presses the urgency of here and now: sense-born pleasures are wombs of pain with beginnings and ends; the real strength is withstanding desire and anger before leaving the body; for the self-controlled seer, the bliss of Brahman lies close on every side.

views.text: The seers are monks of full realization; being engaged in the good of all beings means being favourably disposed to all, that is, harmless.
Chinna-dvaidhāḥ means freed from pairs of opposites like heat and cold; they care for all beings as for their own selves, and so the impurities blocking the self fall away.
The goal is open to those in whom the double knot, of dualism and of doubt, has been cut.
Bodily welfare helps only for a while; the highest welfare is helping others reconnect with God. Purified saints who do this attract more grace and are finally liberated.

verses.hook: What kind of sages work for the welfare of all and attain freedom?

refs.note: Compassion is the natural trait of saints, who use word, mind and body for others' welfare.

verses.devanagari:
कामक्रोधवियुक्तानां यतीनां यतचेतसाम् ।
अभितो ब्रह्मनिर्वाणं वर्तते विदितात्मनाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
kāmakrodhaviyuktānāṃ yatīnāṃ yatacetasām
abhito brahmanirvāṇaṃ vartate viditātmanām
verses.essence: For the ascetics severed from desire and anger, of controlled mind, who know the Self — the nirvana of Brahman lies near, on every side.
verses.translation: Absolute freedom (or Brahmic bliss) exists on all sides for those self-controlled ascetics who are free from desire and anger, who have controlled their thoughts and who have realised the Self.

anvaya.meaning: of those freed from desire and anger
anvaya.base: कामक्रोधवियुक्त · separated from desire and anger
anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + क्रोध (anger) + वियुक्त (separated): those parted from desire and anger
यत (restrained) + चेतस् (mind): those whose mind is restrained
ब्रह्म (Brahman) + निर्वाण (blowing out, peace): the stillness that is Brahman

anvaya.form: verb, present, 3rd person singular, middle voice

anvaya.meaning: of those who know the Self
anvaya.base: विदितात्मन् · one who has known the Self
anvaya.parts: विदित (known) + आत्मन् (Self): those by whom the Self is known

verses.explanation: One word does the work: abhitaḥ — on both sides, all around, here. For the qualified, brahma-nirvāṇa is not a posthumous reward at the end of a corridor; it surrounds them like air, available in life and in death alike. The goal was never far; it was occluded. Remove desire-anger and the unknowing of the Self, and what remains is discovered to have been the environment all along.
verses.connection: Intensifies 5.24–25: for the ready, liberation is not ahead but ambient.
verses.reflection: For one hour, drop desire and anger together and notice freedom standing close on every side.
verses.background: The teaching presses the urgency of here and now: sense-born pleasures are wombs of pain with beginnings and ends; the real strength is withstanding desire and anger before leaving the body; for the self-controlled seer, the bliss of Brahman lies close on every side.

views.text: Abhitaḥ means 'either way': whether living or dead, liberation is there for monks steadfast in full realization, so their release is immediate.
For those practising self-control with mind subdued, the beatitude of Brahman is close at hand, already in their grasp.
For them Brahman-existence holds at every stage and does not wait for the time of formal meditation.

Though karma yoga suits most, true renunciants also progress quickly. Peace depends not on circumstances but on purified senses, mind and intellect, so they find peace everywhere and are liberated here.

verses.hook: Do renunciants who have mastered desire and anger also reach peace?

verses.devanagari:
स्पर्शान्कृत्वा बहिर्बाह्यांश्चक्षुश्चैवान्तरे भ्रुवोः ।
प्राणापानौ समौ कृत्वा नासाभ्यन्तरचारिणौ॥
verses.transliteration:
sparśānkṛtvā bahirbāhyāṃścakṣuścaivāntare bhruvoḥ
prāṇāpānau samau kṛtvā nāsābhyantaracāriṇau
verses.essence: Shutting out external contacts, fixing the gaze between the brows, equalizing the in-breath and out-breath moving within the nostrils —
verses.translation: Shutting out (all) external contacts and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, equalising the outgoing and incoming breaths moving within the nostrils.

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, genitive dual (of the two)
compound noun, masculine, accusative dual (object, the two)
anvaya.parts: प्राण (outgoing breath) + अपान (incoming breath): the two breaths together

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, accusative dual (object, the two)
compound adjective, masculine, accusative dual (object, the two)
anvaya.parts: नासा (nose) + अभ्यन्तर (inside) + चारिन् (moving): the two that move within the nose

verses.explanation: The chapter suddenly hands over a technique — terse as a field manual: world set down at the door, eyes gathered to the brow-center, the two breath-currents evened until they hum at one pitch. After twenty-six verses of vision and principle, two of method: the Gita's reminder that the lotus-leaf state is also a practice with a posture, begun by closing some doors so the inner one can open.
verses.connection: Begins the practical coda (5.27–28): the meditation seed that chapter 6 will grow into a full discipline.
verses.reflection: Sit briefly: gaze settled, breath evened at the doorway of the nostrils — the portable sanctuary.
verses.background: The chapter closes with a thumbnail of meditation — outer contacts shut out, gaze and breath steadied — and then the Gita's celebrated peace formula: knowing Krishna as the enjoyer of all sacrifice, the great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of every being, one attains peace.

views.text: Outer objects are 'kept outside' simply by not attending to the sounds and other objects the senses bring in; no forcible shutting is meant.

The gaze rests between the brows with eyes half-closed: fully closed, the mind sinks into sleep; open, it spills outward. Evening the breaths means checking their up-and-down movement, a form of breath retention.
Fixing the gaze steadies the eyeballs, and rhythmical breathing steadies the mind; when the breath becomes rhythmical the whole system comes into harmony.
Ascetics withdraw from sense objects by fixing the gaze between the eyebrows and balancing the breath. This yields knowledge of the self, but not knowledge of God, which needs devotion.

verses.hook: What meditation practice do ascetics use to shut out the outer world?

verses.devanagari:
यतेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिर्मुनिर्मोक्षपरायणः ।
विगतेच्छाभयक्रोधो यः सदा मुक्त एव सः॥
verses.transliteration:
yatendriyamanobuddhirmunirmokṣaparāyaṇaḥ
vigatecchābhayakrodho yaḥ sadā mukta eva saḥ
verses.essence: — with senses, mind and understanding controlled, intent on liberation, with desire, fear and anger gone: such a sage is forever free.
verses.translation: With the senses, the mind and the intellect (ever) controlled, having liberation as his supreme goal, free from desire, fear and anger the sage is verily liberated for ever.

anvaya.meaning: with senses, mind and intellect controlled
anvaya.base: यतेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धि · one who has mastered senses, mind, intellect
anvaya.parts: यत (controlled) + इन्द्रिय (senses) + मनस् (mind) + बुद्धि (intellect): one whose senses, mind and intellect are controlled

anvaya.base: मोक्षपरायण · having liberation as highest goal
anvaya.parts: मोक्ष (liberation) + परायण (final resort, highest aim): one for whom liberation is the supreme goal

anvaya.meaning: with desire, fear and anger gone
anvaya.base: विगतेच्छाभयक्रोध · free of desire, fear, anger
anvaya.parts: विगत (gone) + इच्छा (desire) + भय (fear) + क्रोध (anger): one from whom desire, fear and anger have gone

verses.explanation: The sentence completes with a tense-shift worth savoring: not 'will be freed' but sadā mukta eva — *ever free*, already. For the one in whom the triple knot (wanting, fearing, raging) has actually dissolved, liberation stops being a future event and is recognized as the standing fact it always was. The practice of 5.27 does not manufacture freedom; it removes what obscured it.
verses.connection: Completes 5.27's technique with its fruit — and the realization that the fruit was never absent.
verses.reflection: Release desire, fear, and anger before one meeting today, and walk in already free.
verses.background: The chapter closes with a thumbnail of meditation — outer contacts shut out, gaze and breath steadied — and then the Gita's celebrated peace formula: knowing Krishna as the enjoyer of all sacrifice, the great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of every being, one attains peace.

views.text: The monk who always remains thus is already free; there is no other liberation left for him to seek.
'Liberated for ever' means he is almost liberated: intent on the vision of the self, he will soon reach the final fruition.
Reading 5.27–28 together, 'the two wandering ones' are desire and wrath, the two breaths are pious and impious acts held in balance, and such a yogi is free even while carrying on worldly business.
The ascetic path of controlling senses, mind and intellect leads to knowledge of the self, yet it is incomplete; to know God it must be fulfilled through devotion, as the next verse says.

verses.hook: What inner state frees the sage seeking liberation for good?

verses.devanagari:
भोक्तारं यज्ञतपसां सर्वलोकमहेश्वरम् ।
सुहृदं सर्वभूतानां ज्ञात्वा मां शान्तिमृच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
bhoktāraṃ yajñatapasāṃ sarvalokamaheśvaram
suhṛdaṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ jñātvā māṃ śāntimṛcchati
verses.essence: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all worlds, the friend of every being — one attains peace.
verses.translation: He who knows Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds and the friend of all beings, attains to peace.

anvaya.base: सर्वलोकमहेश्वर · supreme ruler of all worlds
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + लोक (world) + महा (great) + ईश्वर (lord): the great Lord of all the worlds
सर्व (all) + भूत (being): all beings

verses.explanation: The chapter's last word is a formula for peace in three recognitions — and the third transfigures the first two. The enjoyer of all offerings: so nothing given is lost. The great Lord of all worlds: so nothing is finally out of hand. And then suhṛdaṁ sarva-bhūtānām — the *friend* of every being, who does good without looking for any return. Power that was merely sovereign would awe; power that is also friendship is what lets the grip finally open. Knowing the universe has a friend at its center, one rests: śāntim ṛcchati, one reaches peace.
verses.connection: Closes the chapter by giving its impersonal serenity a face: peace, finally, is trusting whose hands the world is in.
verses.reflection: End the day remembering the friend of all beings — and let that friendship include you.
verses.background: The chapter closes with a thumbnail of meditation — outer contacts shut out, gaze and breath steadied — and then the Gita's celebrated peace formula: knowing Krishna as the enjoyer of all sacrifice, the great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of every being, one attains peace.

views.text: Peace means the complete cessation of transmigration. 'Me' is Nārāyaṇa: the friend who helps all without seeking return, dwells in every heart, dispenses the results of works and witnesses all perception.
Peace here is happiness even while doing karma yoga: knowing the Lord as everyone's friend, one takes up karma yoga gladly as His worship, since all strive to please a friend.
Sense-control alone does not free; knowledge does. Knowing Him as the receiver of what devotees offer and the inner well-wisher of all, one reaches liberation by His grace.
Self-knowledge can come by ascetic practice, but knowledge of God needs His grace through devotion. Knowing Him as enjoyer of all sacrifices, Lord of all and friend of all completes every path.

verses.hook: What must one know about God to reach peace?
